parsed_refs.title: Bioresorbable scaffolds: rationale, current status, challenges, and future

raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to address perceived limitations of permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES): chronic caging of the artery, impaired vasomotion, late neoatherosclerosis, difficulty with future bypass grafting or reintervention, and a continuing, albeit low, risk of very late thrombosis related to durable metal and polymer [1,2]. The concept was biologically attractive because transient radial support and antiproliferative drug delivery could theoretically be followed by restoration of vascular physiology. Early clinical experience with the Igaki-Tamai poly-L-lactic acid scaffold demonstrated feasibility but also the constraints of bulky devices, heat deployment, and restenosis [3,4]. The first widely studied platform, the everolimus-eluting Absorb scaffold, combined a poly-L-lactic acid backbone with a poly-D,L-lactide everolimus coating and was designed for near-complete resorption over approximately 3 years.

The initial Absorb studies generated considerable enthusiasm. In simple de novo lesions, first-in-human and cohort studies showed acceptable late lumen loss, progressive scaffold integration, and signals of vasomotor recovery [5-7]. Multimodality imaging suggested late enlargement of the scaffolded segment and disappearance of struts, supporting the “vascular restoration” hypothesis [8]. These observations, together with evidence that permanent DES failures could be mediated by delayed healing, inflammation, strut malapposition, and neoatherosclerosis [9,10], drove rapid clinical adoption before large definitive outcome data had matured.

Randomized trials subsequently provided a more sobering assessment. ABSORB II compared Absorb with the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent and did not show superiority for vasomotion or late lumen loss; at 3 years, target-lesion failure and device thrombosis were numerically or significantly higher with BVS [11,12]. ABSORB III, a pivotal trial in relatively selected lesions, met its 1-year non-inferiority endpoint, but early safety margins were narrow and later follow-up revealed excess device-oriented events, particularly scaffold thrombosis [13]. ABSORB Japan and ABSORB China broadly confirmed short-term non-inferiority in selected patients but were underpowered for rare safety events [14,15]. ABSORB IV attempted to improve outcomes through stricter lesion selection and implantation technique, demonstrating better early results than earlier experience but not eliminating concern about late events [16].

All-comers and acute coronary syndrome data reinforced these limitations. In AIDA, routine PCI with Absorb was associated with a substantially higher rate of definite or probable device thrombosis than contemporary metallic DES, prompting early safety concern [17]. EVERBIO II and TROFI II showed that BVS could be implanted successfully in broader or STEMI populations, but small sample sizes and imaging-driven endpoints could not establish safety equivalence [18,19]. Meta-analyses of randomized trials consistently found higher scaffold thrombosis and target-vessel myocardial infarction with Absorb, especially beyond 1 year and in small vessels [20-22]. Individual-patient analyses identified vessel size, lesion complexity, diabetes, and suboptimal implantation as important modifiers of risk [23].

Mechanistically, BVS failure is multifactorial. The Absorb scaffold had struts approximately 150 µm thick, increasing flow disturbance and thrombogenicity compared with thin-strut metallic DES [24]. Underexpansion, malapposition, edge dissection, and implantation in vessels smaller than recommended were frequent contributors. Intravascular imaging studies of late and very late scaffold thrombosis demonstrated uncovered or malapposed struts, scaffold discontinuity, restenotic tissue, and intraluminal scaffold dismantling during resorption [25,26]. These findings shifted practice toward meticulous “PSP” technique—adequate lesion preparation, accurate vessel sizing, and high-pressure post-dilatation—preferably guided by intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography. However, improved technique mitigated rather than fully neutralized the intrinsic penalty of bulky bioresorbable struts.

The first-generation Absorb scaffold was withdrawn from routine commercial use, but the broader concept remains active. Magnesium-based resorbable scaffolds offer faster loss of radial strength, more benign degradation products, and improved deliverability. Early magnesium platforms showed feasibility but excessive recoil and restenosis [27]; second-generation sirolimus-eluting absorbable metal scaffolds demonstrated better angiographic and clinical performance in selected lesions [28]. Other polymeric platforms, including novolimus-eluting scaffolds, have also shown promising imaging profiles in early studies [29]. Nonetheless, none has yet demonstrated superiority over best-in-class contemporary DES, which now have thin struts, biocompatible or biodegradable polymers, excellent deliverability, and very low thrombosis rates.

The current role of BVS in PCI is therefore limited. Outside clinical trials, contemporary metallic DES remain the standard for most patients. Future BVS development must solve four linked problems: reducing strut thickness without sacrificing radial strength, controlling dismantling during resorption, improving deliverability in complex anatomy, and proving clinical benefit in adequately powered trials with long-term follow-up. The original rationale—temporary scaffolding followed by vascular restoration—remains compelling, but first-generation experience established that disappearance of the implant is not itself a clinical advantage unless early and late safety match or exceed modern DES. BVS should now be viewed not as a failed idea, but as an instructive technology whose next generation must be judged by hard outcomes rather than biological elegance [30].
